quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten quick checks on creels, cones, bags and why cone size matters for both bulk and sample warps.

questions.q: In the lecture, yarn arrives from the spinner in:
questions.explain: The lecture takes yarn as delivered in 100 lb bags; the bags are divided by the cone weight to find how many cones are available.

questions.q: A 'full creel' means:
options: All the bags have been opened
One complete set of cones, one for every end on the beam
The creel is loaded with as many cones as it can physically hold, regardless of the warp
questions.explain: A full creel is one set of cones equal to the ends per beam (640 here); it is the unit in which yarn can actually be warped.

questions.q: Why can only COMPLETE creels be used?
options: Because a beam needs every one of its ends supplied by a cone
Because partly full cones cannot be wound
Because the sizing machine takes beams in pairs
questions.explain: A warper's beam with some ends missing is useless, so if the cones available do not make up another whole creel of 640, that yarn waits for the next delivery.

questions.q: In the worksheet, 100 bags of yarn are enough to fill four complete creels of 640 cones.
questions.explain: 100 bags give 2,398 cones; 2,398 ÷ 640 = 3.75, so only 3 complete creels can be filled and the remainder (about 20 bags) waits.

questions.q: The lecture's advice for avoiding yarn left over after creeling is to:
options: Order yarn in multiples of the creel requirement
Use an odd number of beams
questions.explain: If each order is a whole number of creel sets, every bag delivered can be used at once instead of 20 bags waiting for the next lot.

questions.q: For a short sample warp, why must the cone be small?
options: Because the sample warper has a small creel
Because a large cone would be mostly wasted after the short sample
Because fine counts cannot be wound on big cones
Because the sample is woven on a narrow loom
questions.explain: A sample needs only a few hundred metres per end; on a 4 lb cone almost all of the yarn would be left over, so the cone should carry just the sample's needs.

questions.q: In the sample-warp calculation, why is the cone size multiplied by the number of beams?
options: Because each beam is sized separately
Because each cone must feed one end on every beam in the set
Because wastage occurs on every beam
questions.explain: The same cone is used for its end on all 6 beams of the set, so it must carry 6 times the length warped on one beam.

questions.q: The 0.155 lb sample cone in the lecture weighs about 70 g.
questions.explain: 0.155 lb × 453.6 g = 70 g, a tiny cone, which is why sample warps are usually made on a sectional or sample warper instead.

questions.q: 'Wastage' in the sample-warp worksheet allows for:
options: Yarn lost in creeling, tying-in and the ends of the warp
The warp crimping in the fabric
questions.explain: Wastage is the extra yarn lost in handling the sample warp; warp contraction is added separately, and size is not part of this calculation.

questions.q: 'Metres of yarn per lb at this count' for Ne 20 is about 15,362. It comes from:
questions.explain: Ne 20 has 840 × 20 = 16,800 yd per lb; × 0.9144 m per yd = 15,362 m per lb.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: The chain from bags to cones to creels, the sample cone formula, and the way each input moves the answer.

questions.q: Cones available from a delivery equals:
questions.explain: Total yarn = bags × 100 lb; dividing by the pounds on one cone gives the number of cones: 100 × 100 ÷ 4.17 ≈ 2,398.

questions.q: Complete creels possible equals:
options: cones available ÷ cones per creel, rounded up
cones available ÷ cones per creel, rounded down
questions.explain: A partial creel cannot be run, so the division is rounded DOWN: 2,398 ÷ 640 = 3.75 → 3 creels.

questions.q: Bags actually used equals:
options: creels × cones per creel × cone size ÷ 100
questions.explain: Cones used = creels × cones per creel; pounds = cones × cone size; bags = pounds ÷ 100: 3 × 640 × 4.17 ÷ 100 = 80.1.

questions.q: With the same bags and creel, a smaller cone size always gives more complete creels.
questions.explain: Smaller cones give more cones, but complete creels are the rounded-down quotient; 2,398 cones give 3 creels, and 2,500 cones (a slightly smaller cone) still give only 3. Creels rise only in steps when another full set of 640 is reached.

questions.q: The warp length to be warped for a sample is:
questions.explain: Both allowances add length: 300 m × 1.2 × 1.1 = 396 m. The fractions must be used as (1 + x), not multiplied bare.

questions.q: Cone size needed for a sample (lb) equals:
options: warp length (m) ÷ beams ÷ metres per lb
warp length (m) × beams ÷ metres per lb
warp length (m) × metres per lb ÷ beams
beams × metres per lb ÷ warp length
questions.explain: Each cone supplies its end on every beam: 396 m × 6 = 2,376 m of yarn; ÷ 15,362 m per lb = 0.155 lb.

questions.q: If the sample count is changed from Ne 20 to Ne 40 with the same lengths and beams, the cone size needed:
questions.explain: Metres per lb doubles (840 × 40 × 0.9144 = 30,724), so the same metres weigh half as much: 0.155 lb becomes 0.077 lb.

questions.q: If the number of beams in the sample set rises from 6 to 8 with everything else fixed, the cone size needed:
questions.explain: Cone size is proportional to the number of beams: 8 ÷ 6 = 1.333, so 0.155 lb becomes 0.206 lb.

questions.q: Cones per creel in the worksheet equals the ends per beam, i.e. total ends ÷ beams.
questions.explain: Each end on a beam needs one cone, so cones per creel = ends per beam = 3,840 ÷ 6 = 640.

questions.q: In the bags-per-creel worksheet the number of beams is found from total ends ÷ creel capacity, rounded up to an even number. Where did that rule come from?
options: Lecture 6, because warper's beams are paired on the sizing creel
Lecture 7, because of the beam volume
questions.explain: The same beam rule as Lecture 6 is used: 3,840 ÷ 840 = 4.57, rounded up to the even number 6.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Bags, cones and creels for a bulk warp, then the cone size for a short sample warp.

questions.q: A fabric has 60 ends per inch, is 63 inches wide and has 60 selvedge ends. How many ends are there in total?
3,840 ends are split over 6 warper's beams. How many cones does one full creel need?
questions.explain: Cones per creel = ends per beam = 3,840 ÷ 6 = 640.

questions.q: 100 bags of 100 lb each are delivered on cones of 4.5 lb. How many whole cones is that?
questions.explain: 10,000 lb ÷ 4.5 lb per cone = 2,222.2, so 2,222 whole cones.

questions.q: 2,222 cones are available and a creel needs 640 cones. How many complete creels can be filled?
questions.explain: 2,222 ÷ 640 = 3.47, rounded down to 3 complete creels; 302 cones are left over.

questions.q: Three creels of 640 cones are run with cones of 4.5 lb. How many 100 lb bags are actually used (to one decimal)?
questions.explain: Cones used = 1,920; × 4.5 lb = 8,640 lb; ÷ 100 = 86.4 bags, leaving 13.6 bags for the next lot.

questions.q: A 300 m sample is required with 20 % wastage and 10 % warp contraction. What length must be warped on each beam, in metres?
How many metres of yarn are there in one pound of Ne 20 cotton yarn (to the nearest 10 m)?
A sample warp of 396 m per beam is to be made on a set of 6 beams in Ne 20 (15,362 m per lb). What cone size is needed, in lb (to three decimals)?
questions.explain: Each cone supplies 396 × 6 = 2,376 m; ÷ 15,362 m per lb = 0.155 lb.

questions.q: A 200 m sample needs 25 % wastage and 8 % contraction, on a set of 4 beams in Ne 30 (23,043 m per lb). What cone size is needed, in lb (to three decimals)?
questions.explain: Warp length = 200 × 1.25 × 1.08 = 270 m; × 4 beams = 1,080 m per cone; ÷ 23,043 = 0.047 lb (about 21 g).

questions.q: A cone of 0.155 lb weighs, in grams, about:
questions.explain: 1 lb = 453.6 g, so 0.155 × 453.6 = 70 g. 155 g would be the figure if a pound were 1,000 g.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Yarn-store and sampling decisions: ordering the right quantity, choosing cone weights and avoiding idle yarn.

questions.q: The yarn store has 100 bags on 4.17 lb cones for a 640-cone creel, and the worksheet shows 80.1 bags used. What happens to the other 20 bags?
options: They wait until the next lot makes up another full creel
They are run on a half-filled creel
They are returned to the spinner
questions.explain: 2,398 cones fill 3 creels (1,920 cones); the remaining 478 cones cannot make a fourth creel of 640, so about 20 bags wait for the next delivery.

questions.q: To use a delivery fully on a 640-cone creel with 4.17 lb cones, how many bags should the next order be, if 4 full creels are wanted?
questions.explain: 4 creels × 640 × 4.17 lb = 10,675 lb ≈ 107 bags; ordering a whole creel multiple avoids left-overs, as the lecture advises.

questions.q: A supplier offers the same yarn on 2.5 kg (5.5 lb) cones instead of 4.17 lb. For the same 100 bags and 640-cone creel, the number of complete creels:
questions.explain: 10,000 ÷ 5.5 = 1,818 cones; ÷ 640 = 2.84 → only 2 complete creels, so even more yarn waits. Bigger cones hold more yarn each but give fewer cones.

questions.q: A merchandiser wants a 300 m sample of fabric A and asks the store to send ordinary 4 lb cones for a 6-beam sample set. The warping manager objects because:
options: 4 lb cones do not fit the sample creel
Only about 0.155 lb per cone is needed, so almost all of each 4 lb cone would be left unused
4 lb cones are too light for a sample
questions.explain: The worksheet gives 0.155 lb per cone; a 4 lb cone is 25 times that, so about 96 % of the yarn on each of the 640 cones would be left after the sample.

questions.q: Making the sample warp on a sectional or sample warper avoids the need for one cone per end of a full-width creel.
questions.explain: The lecture notes sample warps are usually made on a sectional or sample warper for exactly this reason: the tiny 70 g cones a full creel would need are impractical.

questions.q: A planner has 2,398 cones and a creel of 640. She proposes to run a fourth creel with 478 cones and leave the other 162 positions empty. What is wrong?
options: Nothing; the beam will simply have fewer ends
A warper's beam must carry its full complement of ends, so a short creel gives an unusable beam
The warper cannot run with empty creel positions
questions.explain: The beam has to carry 640 ends to match its sisters on the sizing creel and the fabric's total ends; 478 ends would not make the right fabric.

questions.q: For the bulk warp, which change would let the 100 bags be used almost completely?
options: Reducing the cone size so that the cone count becomes a multiple of 640
questions.explain: If the cones from 100 bags came to exactly 4 × 640 = 2,560, i.e. 3.9 lb per cone, all four creels could run and nearly nothing would wait. Wastage, selvedges and contraction do not change the creel arithmetic.

questions.q: A sample of 300 m is requested but the sample set is to be run on 2 beams instead of 6 (a narrower sample). The cone size needed:
questions.explain: Cone size is proportional to beams: 396 × 2 ÷ 15,362 = 0.052 lb, one third of the 6-beam figure.

questions.q: A yarn store reports it has 'enough yarn for the order' because the total pounds match the warp weight. The warping manager still refuses to start. The likely reason is:
options: The pounds are on too few cones to fill a complete creel
The yarn is in bags rather than cartons
questions.explain: Total weight is not enough: the yarn must be on at least as many cones as the creel has positions (640), each holding enough length. Weight on too few cones cannot be creeled.

questions.q: Which quantity in the sample-warp worksheet would you reduce first to cut the cone size, without changing the fabric or sample length?
questions.explain: Wastage is the only allowance under the warper's control; contraction belongs to the fabric, and count and metres per lb are fixed by the yarn.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Harder two-step problems on creels, cones and sample warps, and the slips that most often spoil the answer.

questions.q: A fabric has 72 EPI, is 66 inches wide with 48 selvedge ends, on an 840-cone creel. How many cones does one full creel need (ends per beam, with beams rounded up to even)?
questions.explain: Total ends = 72 × 66 + 48 = 4,800; ÷ 840 = 5.7 → 6 beams; 4,800 ÷ 6 = 800 cones per creel.

questions.q: 150 bags of 100 lb on 4 lb cones are delivered for a creel of 800 cones. How many complete creels can be filled?
questions.explain: 15,000 ÷ 4 = 3,750 cones; ÷ 800 = 4.69 → 4 complete creels (3,200 cones); 550 cones wait.

questions.q: With 4 creels of 800 cones at 4 lb each, how many bags are used?
questions.explain: 3,200 cones × 4 lb = 12,800 lb = 128 bags; 22 bags of the 150 are left over.

questions.q: A student calculates complete creels as 2,398 ÷ 640 = 3.75 and rounds UP to 4, then reports 106.8 bags used from a delivery of 100. The error is:
options: Creels must be rounded down; a fourth creel cannot be filled, so 3 creels and 80.1 bags
questions.explain: A partial creel is useless, so the quotient is rounded down to 3; 106.8 bags also exceeds the 100 bags delivered, which should have flagged the mistake.

questions.q: A 400 m sample needs 20 % wastage and 10 % contraction on a 6-beam set in Ne 40 (30,724 m per lb). What cone size is required, in lb (to three decimals)?
Doubling the sample length from 300 m to 600 m doubles the cone size needed, all else equal.
questions.explain: Cone size is proportional to the warp length per beam, which is proportional to the sample length; 0.155 lb becomes 0.309 lb.

questions.q: A sample cone is calculated as 396 ÷ 15,362 = 0.026 lb. What has been forgotten?
options: The multiplication by the 6 beams each cone must feed
The conversion from yards to metres
questions.explain: 396 m is the length per beam; the cone feeds its end on all 6 beams, so 396 × 6 ÷ 15,362 = 0.155 lb. Wastage is already inside the 396 m.

questions.q: An Ne 20 sample cone of 0.155 lb is available only as a 0.5 lb cone. Roughly what fraction of the yarn on each cone will be left after the 6-beam sample?
questions.explain: 0.155 ÷ 0.5 = 31 % is used, so about 69 % of each cone is left over, which is why oversize sample cones are wasteful.

questions.q: How many bags of 100 lb are needed to fill exactly 5 creels of 640 cones with 4.17 lb cones (to one decimal)?
questions.explain: 5 × 640 = 3,200 cones × 4.17 lb = 13,344 lb = 133.4 bags; ordering in such creel multiples avoids idle yarn.

questions.q: For fabric A (3,840 ends, 6 beams) a mill switches to a 1,000-cone creel. Using the Lecture 6 rule, the beam plan and cones per creel become:
questions.explain: 3,840 ÷ 1,000 = 3.84, rounded up to the even number 4; 3,840 ÷ 4 = 960 cones per creel, which fits inside the 1,000-cone creel.
